UNDERSTAND THE FLOW

THE BURGERS VORTEX

A swirl.
With a structure.

Imagine a drop of dye in moving water. It spirals toward a central axis, then stretches upward or downward. The strands make those paths visible.

What you are seeing

The paths are based on a Burgers vortex: an idealized, steady flow connected to the Navier–Stokes equations. These equations relate fluid motion to pressure and viscosity.

∂u/∂t + (u · ∇)u = −∇p/ρ + ν∇²u

For an incompressible fluid: ∇ · u = 0. Here u is velocity, p is pressure, ρ is density, and ν is kinematic viscosity.

Try it yourself

Open the Explorer. Increase swirl for tighter winding, or increase viscosity for a wider core. Rotate the model to compare the shapes.

Explore in 3D ↗

Where the art begins

Strand thickness and proportions are adjusted for clarity. The particle assembly, twisting and light pulses are artistic effects, not a simulation of a vortex forming over time. This is a visual study, not a solution to the Millennium Prize Problem.

SHAPE & FLOW

A fruit fly.
Up close.

How to explore

Choose an object and watch the flow around it. Drag to inspect its shape. Use Side view to compare the silhouette with the calculated flow.

Trails
Particles follow the calculated velocity field.
Speed
Cool to warm colors show slower to faster flow relative to the inlet.
Vorticity
Blue and orange show opposite directions of local rotation.

What the number means

Wake slowdown is the average loss of horizontal speed at a fixed section behind the object, compared with the inlet. It is a local indicator, not a drag coefficient or an aerodynamic score.

The browser calculates 2D flow around a fixed side silhouette using the lattice Boltzmann method. The 3D model is for inspection. Sizes are illustrative; wing flapping, lift and downforce are not simulated.

VORTEX / PROJECT

ABOUT THIS PROJECT

See the shape
of flow.

VORTEX is an interactive study of fluid motion. Explore a 3D vortex, adjust its parameters, and compare flow around a fruit fly, a Formula 1 car and an aircraft.

The live scenes run in WebGL. Blender was used to prepare the models and the formation film.

Models & sources

The vortex starts from the Burgers flow model. The wind tunnel uses a 2D lattice Boltzmann solver. The fruit fly comes from NeuroMechFly (NeLy, EPFL), adapted for this scene under Apache 2.0. The car and aircraft are original procedural models.
